problems.title: Clockwise triangular cycle: net work

body.md: A monatomic ideal gas is taken around a clockwise cycle $ABCA$ on a $P$-$V$ diagram. State $A$ is at $V_A = 2.0\ \text{m}^3$, $P_A = 15\ \text{Pa}$; state $B$ is at $V_B = 6.0\ \text{m}^3$, $P_B = 35\ \text{Pa}$; and state $C$ is at $V_C = 6.0\ \text{m}^3$, $P_C = 15\ \text{Pa}$. Path $AB$ is a straight line, $BC$ is vertical, and $CA$ is horizontal.

body.alt: Pressure against volume: a right triangle ABCA with A at lower left, B at upper right and C below B, traced clockwise.

problems.ask: What is the net work done on the gas after one complete cycle ABCA, in J?

wrong.hint: QUACK. That number is from the practice exam. New numbers here.
QUACK. The height of the triangle is the pressure difference, not the pressure at B.
QUACK. Check both the triangle area factor of one-half and the clockwise sign rule.
QUACK. The path forms a triangle, not a rectangle. Remember the factor of one-half in triangle area.
QUACK. You found only the work along segment AB. Include the return path along CA to complete the cycle.
QUACK. A clockwise cycle on a pressure-volume graph gives negative work done on the gas. Check your sign.

saccharine.title: Clockwise triangular cycle: net work
saccharine.tip: On a $P$-$V$ diagram, the magnitude of net cycle work is the enclosed area, and a clockwise loop gives negative work on the gas.
saccharine.key:
Triangle area $= \frac{1}{2}(6.0 - 2.0)(35 - 15) = 40.0\ \text{J}$.
Clockwise cycle gives negative work on the gas.
Answer: -40.0 J

problems.title: Spring and mass: period factor

body.md: A mass hangs on a spring and oscillates in simple harmonic motion. The mass is then replaced by one that is $2.80$ times heavier. The same spring is used.

body.alt: Two copies of the same spring hanging from a ceiling, the left one carrying a mass m and the right one a larger block of mass 2.80 times m.

problems.ask: By what factor does the period change (new period divided by old period)?

wrong.hint: QUACK. You squared where you should take a square root. The period goes as the root of the mass.
QUACK. The period does not grow in step with the mass. The mass sits under a square root.
QUACK. More mass does not shorten the period. It makes each swing slower.
QUACK. Two slips: the period gets longer with more mass, and it goes with a square root, not a square.
QUACK. You halved the mass factor instead of taking its square root.
QUACK. You turned the ratio upside down. More mass makes the oscillation slower, so the period gets longer.

saccharine.title: Spring and mass: period factor
saccharine.tip: Write the period formula for the old and new mass and divide. Everything except the mass cancels.
